title: VOID MANTICORE
summary: VOID MANTICORE is a Microsoft-assigned designation for an Iranian-nexus intrusion set tracked elsewhere as COBALT MYSTIQUE, Handala Hack, Homeland Justice, Karma, Karmabelow80, BANISHED KITTEN and Red Sandstorm, with public reporting noting overlaps between these names rather than proving they are one identical team. Reporting describes a mix of espionage and hack-and-leak activity: credential phishing against mail and identity services, abuse of virtual private network appliances and exposed remote access, and destructive or disruptive operations against government and public services in several countries. The group's public-facing persona has been used to claim attacks and publish stolen material, which means the leak channel itself becomes evidence. Because the naming overlaps are contested, defenders should treat the aliases as reporting-dependent clusters and check each source's scope. Observed artefacts include mass phishing pages that imitate single sign-on portals, mailbox rule and forwarding changes, abnormal authentication from foreign addresses, and wiper or defacement activity on targeted endpoints.

beginner.definition: VOID MANTICORE is the name one security company uses for an attacker group linked to Iran by public reporting. Other companies and news reports use names such as Handala Hack, Homeland Justice and Karma. The group steals information and also tries to damage or embarrass the organisations it attacks.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group mixes spying with public humiliation. It steals emails, then publishes them to cause anger and distrust. It has also damaged systems so that services stop working. For a public body, the damage to reputation can last longer than the technical repair. Because the same group has many names, defenders can miss related activity.
howItWorks: The group builds a copy of a company login page that looks real.
It sends email that pushes staff to that page and collects the password.
With the stolen password, it reads mail and quietly adds hidden rules.
It also looks for weak remote access, such as an old network device.
Stolen material is saved and later published under a public persona.
In some reported cases, it also destroys data or breaks services.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk where someone photocopies private letters. The thief does not take money or medicine. Instead, the copies are pinned to the front door the next morning, where patients and staff can read them. The building still works, but trust is broken and everyone feels exposed. That mix of theft and public display is what makes this group different.
takeaways: One attacker group can carry several vendor names, so link activity by behaviour, not only by name.
Multi-factor authentication stops most password phishing from turning into mailbox access.
Check mailbox forwarding rules and new administrator accounts after any suspected phishing.

objectives: Explain how a hack-and-leak campaign differs from a purely financial attack.
Describe the credential phishing chain that leads to mailbox access.
Recognise the account settings attackers change to keep reading mail quietly.
Explain why alias overlap between vendors makes attribution difficult and contested.
List the evidence sources that support an investigation into this group's activity.
Outline the first response steps after a suspected destructive intrusion.
